d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of rhapsodize.
To speak with exaggerated or rapturous enthusiasm (about, (up)on or over something).
d.x: How can one rhapsodise over a view when surrounded by beer-stained tables? How lose one’s self in historical reverie amid the odour of roast veal and spinach?

d.g: To say (something) with exaggerated or rapturous enthusiasm.
d.x: “Listen, my pearl,” he rhapsodized. “I have money now and you shall have dresses like rainbows, a gold tiara and slave girls to wait on you […]”

d.g: To recount or describe (something) as a rhapsody, or in the manner of a rhapsody.
d.x: The great poetry of the opening chapter of Ulysses […] amplifies and rhapsodizes the world with an unlooked-for accuracy and transport.

d.g: To perform a rhapsody.
d.x: […] Carolan, the last of the Irish bards, rhapsodized in the halls of the O’Connors so lately as the year 1730.
